newsitem.title: USA: Clinton makes children a priority in health rules.
newsitem.headline: Clinton makes children a priority in health rules.

text.p: The White House said Monday it would make meeting the special needs and sensitivities of children a priority when setting health, safety and environmental regulations.
"This executive order says to every federal agency and department: Put our children first," Vice President Al Gore told a news conference at Children's National Medical Centre.
"From now on, agencies will have to take a hard look at the special risks and disproportionate impact that standards and safeguards have on children," Gore said.

President Clinton signed the order, which directs agencies to make the protection of children a high priority, requires agencies to analyse and explain effects of their rules on children and creates an administration task force for research on children's health and environmental issues.

"It directs federal departments and agencies to step back from the normal regulatory, rulemaking and standard-setting process and ensure that, at the end of the day, our children are protected from environmental risks and safety risks," Carol Browner, administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency, told the news conference.
Browner last year directed her agency to see that its new rules made children's health a priority and this year she started an Office of Children's Health Protection.

Other agencies affected by the White House order include the Health and Human Services Department, the Food and Drug Administration, the Consumer Products Safety Commission, the Transportation Department, the Housing Department and the Agriculture Department.

The interagency task force is to seek public comment and develop an agenda for research on children's health and safety issues. The White House Office of Management and Budget is to organise an inter-agency forum that will produce an annual summary of statistics and indicators of the well-being of the nation's children.

"It's a positive step, but the agencies have to carry it out in a way that's meaningful and aggressive and in the face of industry opposition, and the first great test of that is the Clean Air rule," Greg Wetstone, legislative affairs director of the Natural Resources Defence Council, said.

The EPA has proposed strengthening air quality standards, a move the environmental community is promoting while industry groups say the new standards would cost billions of dollars and cause economic havoc.
The administration is to announce a final decision on the new standards in July.
